title: customer-facing-degradation-communication-guidelines
content:
Purpose:
Quick reference and draft language for customer-facing communications when inference quality, latency, or availability degrade. Focus: concise, trust-building, and prescriptive (what customers can expect + how we mitigate).

Audience and use cases:
- Customer success & account teams: rapid email/Slack templates for impacted customers.
- Product marketing: standardized messaging blocks for status page, support docs, and release notes.
- Sales/AE: short high-level reassurance lines for enterprise buyers.
- Engineering/Oncall: canonical taxonomy for what to say while engineers focus on root cause.

High-level messaging principles (keep short):
- Transparency: what happened in plain language (no technical jargon unless audience is eng).
- Ownership: what Redwood is doing right now; who’s owning the fix.
- Impact-first: summarize customer impact up front (regions, models, percent of requests).
- Triage & timeline: next checkpoints and expected update cadence.
- Mitigation & workarounds: immediate steps customers can take and automated fallbacks we enable.
- Forward commitments: follow-up post-incident analysis (RCA/lessons).

Example single-sentence lead lines (vary by audience):
- Engineers/Platform: "We've identified increased tail latency for model X in us-west1; traffic is being routed to our warmed canary pool in eu-west1 to preserve throughput while we remediate."
- Product/Business: "Some requests are experiencing delays; we're routing traffic to alternate regions and enabling lower-latency fallbacks to keep your app responsive."
- Executive/C-Level: "Service performance is impacted for a small subset of requests; we've activated cross-region routing and prioritization rules to maintain availability."

Fallback taxonomy (operationally useful categories):
- Tier 0: Transparent degradation (no behavior change). Only internal alerting; notify affected customers for business-critical SLAs.
- Tier 1: Latency mitigation. Enable model-variant fallback to quantized/fast path (auto-enabled per-policy). Notify via status page and account rep if >1 minute.
- Tier 2: Feature-limited mode. Disable non-critical features (tool-calls, large-context generation) and keep core text outputs. Send customer email template.
- Tier 3: Regional failover. Route traffic to alternate region with compatible model. For Private deployments, recommend enabling standby region or Dedicated overflow.
- Tier 4: Degraded safety/quality tradeoff (last-resort). Use conservative prompt-safety bypass only with customer opt-in and clear notice.

Multi-region messaging guidance:
- Lead with scope: "affected region(s): us-west1" and "customers in region X may see increased latency".
- Explain routing: "We route to eu-west1 as a resilient experience tier; data residency note if applicable."
- Cost/latency tradeoffs: mention potential cost or latency differences when routed cross-region.
- For Private/Dedicated: "If you require strict region residency, we recommend enabling dedicated standby capacity or our private multi-zone option."

Incident narrative templates (short, reusable):
- Initial alert (status page/Slack):
  "Incident: Elevated latency for text-generation in us-west1. Impact: ~7% of requests see >2x latency. Action: routing to eu-west1, spinning additional capacity, investigating root cause. Next update in 20 minutes. (Owner: Eng-SRE)"

- Customer email (concise):
  "Subject: Brief service update — short-term latency issue

  Hi [Customer],

  We detected higher-than-normal response times for some requests in the us-west1 region starting at 09:18 UTC. To minimize impact we routed requests to an alternate region and enabled fast-path fallbacks for affected models. You may notice slightly different latencies or model behavior during this period. Our on-call and runtime teams are actively investigating and we'll send a follow-up with root cause and remediation steps by EOD.

  If you have production traffic that must not be cross-routed, reply and we will prioritize a private failover plan for your account.

  — Aisha on behalf of Redwood Inference"

- Post-incident summary (public-facing):
  "Summary: On 2024-11-07 we observed transient performance degradation affecting model X in us-west1. Cause: overload on the kernel scheduling layer triggered cascading queuing; fix: adjusted kernel selector heuristics and increased canary capacity. Impact: brief latency increases for ~7% of requests between 09:18–09:42 UTC. Customer-facing mitigations included cross-region routing and model-variant fallbacks. Next steps: extended regression tests and additional guardrails in our routing policy. Full RCA: internal link."

Competitive/positioning notes (how to differentiate in messaging):
- Against managed endpoint providers: emphasize active runtime-level fallbacks (auto model-variant & routing) vs. manual scaling. "We automatically route and fall back to preserve availability while you focus on product."
- Against self-hosted runtimes: stress public SLA + opaque private options; selling point: "same API and rollout controls whether hosted or private, with predictable cost/latency tradeoffs."
- Against single-region vendors: highlight multi-region failover, transparent customer controls, and region-aware privacy options.
- Avoid direct vendor bashing; use comparative statements that focus on outcomes (latency SLOs, automated fallbacks, predictable economics).

On what to say (dos and don'ts):
- DO: Acknowledge impact, provide immediate mitigation steps, commit to a timeline for next update.
- DO: Use clear measurable terms (percent of requests, time windows).
- DO: Offer concrete options to customers (private standby, dedicated capacity).
- DON'T: Overpromise exact ETA for root cause. Say "investigating" not "fixed shortly" unless confident.
- DON'T: Leak internal tools or complex implementation details to non-technical customers.

Support & escalation play (quick checklist):
- T+0: On-call posts status page entry + Slack #customer-engaged; assign owner.
- T+5min: Enable automatic routing/fallback policies; throttle/limit non-critical workloads.
- T+15min: Notify account reps for customers with active sessions or SLAs.
- T+60min: Customer email with initial mitigation summary + ETA for full update.
- Post-recovery: Schedule RCA review with affected customers if enterprise.

Suggested language snippets for status page components (short):
- "We are experiencing elevated latency in us-west1. We have enabled cross-region routing to maintain availability for most customers."
- "Partial degradation: core inference remains available, non-essential features may be limited."

Open questions / decisions needed: (TO-DOs)
- How to surface cost implications to customers automatically when cross-region routing occurs? (Linked ticket: JIRA-INC-2251)
- Decide on customer opt-in vs opt-out defaults for last-resort quality tradeoffs. (policy decision required)
- Where to host canned RCAs for public consumption vs private (per-customer) RCAs?

Next steps (owners):
- Finalize templates for Account Execs and CS (owner: Marco Chen, due 2024-12-08).
- Wire short status snippets into console status page feed (owner: Product Console, PR #812).
- Draft billing/opt-in language for cross-region routing (owner: Ravi Srinivasan).

Notes to self (brief):
- Keep examples short; GTM hates long prose in incident emails.
- Validate template with 2 enterprise customers (ask CS to run a tabletop).
- Reference runtime team's fallback naming (model-variant vs. fast-path) to avoid inconsistent terms.

References and quick links:
- Incident runbooks (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPER/incident-runbooks
- Routing & fallback design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/routing-fallbacks
- Rails for customer comms: https://docs.redwood.ai/go-to-market/comm-rails

(END)
